\section{Introduction}\label{sec:1}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{1}

Child stunting remains one of the most persistent markers of population health disadvantage in Sub-Saharan Africa. Linear growth faltering is concentrated in the first two years of life, is difficult to reverse once established, and its consequences extend well beyond anthropometry to cognitive development, school attainment, and adult earning capacity \autocite{Victora2008,Victora2010,Black2013}. Water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) conditions occupy a central place among the exposures proposed to explain this variation, via several biologically plausible, separately evidenced mechanisms reviewed in full in Section 2.1. Even the strongest recent causal evidence against basic WASH interventions reducing stunting does not dispute this plausibility (Section 2.3); plausibility is not the same claim as an established causal mechanism, and this thesis does not conflate the two. What is considerably less settled is whether the mechanism translates into a \emph{detectable, policy-relevant statistical association} in observational survey data once household wealth and local development are accounted for, and whether a \emph{basic facility-level} WASH classification, rather than a comprehensive intervention package, is the right exposure in which to look for it --- the empirical question this thesis addresses.

\subsection{Two distinct exposures: household facilities and surroundings}\label{sec:1.1}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.1}

A household's own water source and sanitation facility are not the only WASH-related exposure a child faces: even a child with an improved latrine and piped water can be exposed through shared water sources, open defecation by neighbours, or proximity to inadequately managed waste if the surrounding community lacks similar facilities. \emph{Own-household WASH} and \emph{surrounding-community WASH} correspond to two different exposure pathways, not a modelling convenience. Improved household sanitation is a textbook source of a local environmental externality, since it reduces the pathogen load the household releases into the shared environment, and recent research \autocite{Donohue2023,SkoufiasVinha2026} suggests household and community WASH need not move together or carry the same association with child growth. The thesis therefore constructs and compares both: a child's own household classification, and a leave-one-out measure of improved-facility coverage among all \emph{other} households in the same DHS cluster.

\subsection{Exposure timing in cross-sectional survey designs}\label{sec:1.2}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.2}

A measurement limitation affects the cross-sectional, repeated-survey-round literature this baseline analysis belongs to \autocite{Rakotomanana2020,Addae2024}: household and community WASH status is recorded once, at the survey date, and applied to every child regardless of age, so a four-year-old's WASH measurement describes conditions years after their nutritionally critical first two years, while an infant's describes conditions close to their own early life. This does not apply to the major WASH trials, which assign exposure near birth and follow growth prospectively (Section 2.3), nor to panel designs tracking indicators over successive rounds (Section 2.2). Age controls and age-interaction tests, also estimated here, describe how the \emph{current} association varies with a child's age today; they do not reconstruct a child's actual early-life environment. The baseline analysis documents this limitation and does not claim to resolve it.

A separate, bounded extension responds to one dimension of it. It does not ask whether assigning a \emph{historical} instead of a \emph{current} exposure changes an otherwise identical estimate --- the baseline and historical samples differ too much in other respects to isolate that comparison (Section 6.2). Instead it asks, within its own sample: \emph{is modelled local WASH coverage during a child's own early-life window associated with later anthropometric outcomes?} It matches each child's birth-cohort location to a modelled WASH coverage surface for a defined early-life window, using IHME's gridded 2000--2017 estimates \autocite{LBDWaSH2020}, giving genuine within-cluster, cross-birth-cohort variation a single survey round cannot offer --- an improvement on timing specifically, not a record of a child's actual household facilities. It carries its own separate limitations (Section 1.6; Section 6).

\subsection{Research questions and scope}\label{sec:1.3}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.3}

This thesis asks three questions, each posed and answered as an \emph{association under a cross-sectional design}, not a causal effect: (1) is a child's own household water/sanitation status associated with HAZ/WAZ/WHZ after household- and cluster-level confounding is accounted for; (2) is the surrounding community's WASH status, independent of the household, separately associated with these outcomes; (3) within the three historical-sample countries, is modelled local WASH coverage during a child's early-life window associated with these outcomes? The third question is answered only within the historical sample; its answer is not compared with the first two as if that isolated an exposure-timing effect (Section 6.2).

The baseline pools each country's most recent DHS round: Ethiopia (2024--25), Ghana (2022), Kenya (2022), Nigeria (2024), selected for data availability and recency, not as a representative sample of Sub-Saharan Africa. The historical extension uses an earlier round for three of the four (Ghana 2014, Kenya 2014, Nigeria 2018), linked to IHME's gridded estimates; Ethiopia's 2016 round enters only as a provisional sensitivity analysis, because its interview-date conversion could not be fully validated (Section 3.5, Appendix C). The baseline and historical samples are \emph{not the same children}, use different exposure definitions, and are analysed and reported separately; no result in one adjusts, selects, or validates a result in the other.

\subsection{Contribution}\label{sec:1.4}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.4}

This thesis makes two separate contributions in two separate samples, not one combined design. In the \emph{baseline sample}, the contribution is the explicit, side-by-side construction and comparison of own-household and leave-one-out community WASH exposure within one four-country sample and one consistent control set, each exposure estimated under the fixed-effects structure its own construction requires (Sections 4.2--4.3). In the \emph{historical sample}, the contribution is a transparently documented, preliminary attempt to introduce genuine temporal variation in early-life exposure through geospatial matching (Sections 3.5--3.8); it does not reproduce the household-versus-community comparison, since the historical data source does not distinguish a child's household from its surroundings. A particular four-country combination is not, by itself, evidence of substantive novelty, and this thesis does not claim it as such; the methodological limitations of each sample are treated as integral to its interpretation, not as closing caveats.

\subsection{A restrained summary of findings}\label{sec:1.5}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.5}

Household-level WASH shows no statistically significant association with any outcome under cluster fixed effects. Community-level WASH coverage shows a large, significant association before covariate adjustment that attenuates to insignificance once socioeconomic and region controls are added, consistent with, though not proof of, confounding by local conditions. Within the historical sample, the pooled established-date water--HAZ association is positive and significant, but sensitive to the pooled weighting convention and carries unresolved documentation issues. None of these results identifies a causal policy effect or cost-effectiveness; Sections 5--6 develop them with full uncertainty, and the Abstract gives exact coefficients.

\subsection{Principal limitations, stated at the outset}\label{sec:1.6}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{1.6}

This is a cross-sectional, associational design throughout, not a panel, difference-in-differences, or instrumental-variables design. The principal limitations, stated in full in Section 6, are unresolved sampling-weight documentation for the historical extension's measured-anthropometry subsample, DHS/IHME input overlap in two of its three countries, current residence as a proxy for historical residence, confidentiality-driven displacement of DHS cluster coordinates, and the small number of countries in both samples.
